title: Demonstrate an understanding of a general business plan and adapt it to a selected business idea

lessons.title: What a business plan is
lessons.html:
A map for your business

A business plan is a written plan that explains what your business will do, how it will do it, and how it will make money. It is like a map. It helps you think clearly before you spend money. Banks, the Land Bank, development agencies and investors usually ask for a business plan before they give a loan or a grant.

Finding a business idea

A good idea solves a need that people will pay for. Look around you:

  • Are people buying vegetables from far away because nobody grows them locally?
  • Do farmers in the area need someone to shear sheep, fix fences or spray crops?
  • Is there a demand for eggs, broilers or seedlings in the village?

Choose an idea you understand, can afford to start, and that has customers nearby.

The main parts of a business plan

  1. Summary: a short description of the whole plan.
  2. The business: name, owner(s), type of business and where it is.
  3. Product or service: what you will sell.
  4. Market: who your customers are, how many there are, and who your competitors are.
  5. Marketing: price, how customers will hear about you, and how you will deliver.
  6. Operations: what you need to produce: land, equipment, inputs, workers.
  7. Money (financial plan): start-up costs, monthly costs, expected sales and profit.
  8. Risks: what could go wrong and what you will do about it.

A plan does not need to be long. A few clear pages are better than many pages of guessing.

lessons.title: Adapting the plan to a broiler business
lessons.html:
Example: Lerato's broiler business

Lerato wants to raise broiler chickens on her family's land near Polokwane and sell them live and slaughtered to people in the village and to a local butchery. Here is how she adapts the general plan to her idea.

Business and product

Sole trader, Lerato's Chickens. Product: broilers sold at about six weeks old, live or slaughtered and cleaned.

Market

Customers: families in the village, especially at month-end and for weddings and funerals; one butchery that wants 100 birds a month. Competitors: supermarket frozen chicken in town and two other sellers. Her advantage is fresh chicken close to home.

Operations

  • A small chicken house for 200 birds, with feeders, drinkers and a heater for the first weeks.
  • Day-old chicks bought from a reputable hatchery, feed, vaccines as advised by the supplier or vet, and wood shavings.
  • Her brother helps with feeding and cleaning.

Simple financial plan for one batch

ItemAmount (R)
200 day-old chicks2 000
Feed9 000
Vaccines, shavings, electricity, transport1 500
Total costs12 500
Sales: 190 birds x R8015 200
Profit per batch2 700

These figures are only an example. Lerato must check real prices in her area. She expects some birds to die, so she plans to sell 190, not 200. Start-up costs for the house and equipment are separate and must be paid back over time.

Risks

Disease, feed price increases, theft, and power cuts. Her plans: good hygiene and vaccinations, buying feed in bulk with neighbours, a lockable house, and a gas heater as backup.

Review the plan

After each batch Lerato compares real costs and sales with her plan and changes it.

Key points

  • A business plan explains what you sell, to whom, how and for what profit.
  • Main parts: business, product, market, marketing, operations, money and risks.
  • Adapt the general plan to your own idea with real local figures.
  • Plan for losses and risks.
  • Review and update the plan regularly.
